# Closing: a world that shrank unevenly {.unnumbered}

It is tempting to tell this story as one smooth acceleration. The maps say otherwise.

The shrinking was uneven in time. For more than fifteen centuries travel barely changed, and in some ways it went backwards: a Roman in Lutetia could reach Rome faster than a Parisian in 1300. Then, in little more than a century, from the turgotine coaches of the 1770s to the steamships and railways of the 1850s, the old limits fell one after another.

It was uneven in space. Every map in this document shows fast corridors and slow gaps: the Rhône and the sea lanes for the Romans, the post roads for the diligence, the first railway spokes around Paris in 1850, the air routes of 1950. Being near a line mattered more than being near Paris.

It was uneven between people. The fastest journey was almost always a privilege: the state post of Rome, the first-class-only Orient Express, the Collins liners with no steerage, Concorde's hundred seats. Most travellers, from the Bordeaux Pilgrim to the emigrants of Le Havre, moved at the slower pace below the headline figures. Only in the last half century has fast travel become ordinary.

And from 1794, the story split in two. News began to outrun people with Chappe's telegraph and crossed the oceans with the cable of 1866. Since then the maps in this document describe the movement of people; news has travelled on its own, almost instantly.

The last chapter adds a final twist. Since the 1970s, long-distance travel times have stopped falling. The world did not keep shrinking; it filled up instead, with nearly five billion air passengers a year. The next change may not be speed at all, but how much travel the world can afford.
